nature-econ-342.title: Markets: where buyers meet sellers
nature-econ-342.text: Markets range from one building's food market to a city's housing market, a whole country, or worldwide trades such as diamonds. A market is any arrangement that lets buyers and sellers exchange goods, services and information. Each exchange, with or without money, is called a transaction. Most markets rely on sellers swapping goods or labor for buyers' money rather than on barter. A market can arise more or less on its own or be built on purpose. Economists see it as a coordinating mechanism: it uses prices to pass information among firms, households and individuals, and that use of prices is its defining feature. By letting tradeable things be valued and priced, markets spread resources around a society. Some markets are even created by regulation to tackle side effects such as pollution, for example markets in pollution permits. Markets can also go wrong. When a market's equilibrium is not efficient, economists say a market failure has occurred, though government fixes can fail too. A seller or buyer with the power to sway prices ({{ref:nature-econ-397}}) can distort them, which lowers welfare and efficiency.

nature-econ-356.title: Price: where buyers and sellers agree
nature-econ-356.text: In April 2020 the price of West Texas Intermediate crude oil for May delivery turned negative for the first time, at -$37.63 a barrel. That strange day tests the definition of a price. A price is the amount of money buyers are willing and able to pay for a good or service, and that sellers are willing to accept. Prices are shaped by production costs, by supply and by demand. A single seller may set them, or market conditions may impose them. Price theory says that in a market left free, the price settles where the quantity supplied equals the quantity demanded. Price and cost are different things. Price is what the buyer pays, while cost of production is the seller's own spending on making the product. Milton Friedman named five functions of prices, among them passing on information, giving incentives to produce what is valued, and rationing fixed supplies among consumers. Prices also posed an old puzzle. Adam Smith's diamond–water paradox asks why diamonds cost more than water, though water is essential to life and diamonds are mere ornament. Carl Menger's theory of marginal utility was offered as one answer.

nature-econ-344.title: Willingness to pay: the most you would hand over
nature-econ-344.text: People will pay more for the same soft drink at a luxury resort than at a beach bar or a local shop. Willingness to pay is the highest price at which a person will definitely buy one unit of something, and as the soft drink shows, it depends on context. It matches the standard economic idea of a consumer's reservation price, though some researchers treat it as a range. The idea has a long public history. Jules Dupuit argued that a bridge, road or canal is worth the sum of what its users would pay. Adding up their willingness to pay, he said, measures its social benefit. Today, {{ref:nature-val-001}} does the same, turning hard-to-price impacts into money, though the amounts are often hard to estimate. For nature, survey methods such as {{ref:nature-val-085}} simply ask people what they would pay for an ecosystem or one of its services. A related measure, {{ref:nature-val-019}}, estimates how much people would pay to lower their risk of dying, and is used to cost deaths from air pollution. One wrinkle runs through all of this. People's maximum willingness to pay for an object is typically lower than the least they would accept to give it up once they own it.

nature-econ-369.title: Demand: wanting something and being able to pay
nature-econ-369.text: Demand is not the same as desire. In economics it means both wanting something and being able to pay for it. Demand is the quantity of a good that people are willing and able to buy at various prices over a given period. It is a flow, measured per unit of time, not a single purchase. The most important influence is the good's own price. Normally, the lower the price, the more people buy. Demand also depends on the prices of complements and substitutes, income, tastes, expectations, population size, climate and government policy. Expectations matter more than they might seem. If consumers expect a price rise, they buy more now to avoid paying more later. Goods with no substitutes, such as insulin, have nearly perfectly inelastic demand: price barely changes how much is bought. Not everyone accepts demand as the goal. {{ref:nature-hist-060}} challenged the idea that meeting demand is the purpose of economic activity, separating wise demands for genuine needs from unwise ones.

nature-econ-412.title: Supply: what sellers will offer
nature-econ-412.text: Farmers, factories and workers looking for jobs all answer the same question: how much will they offer at a given price? Supply is the amount of something that producers, workers or other sellers are willing and able to offer for sale. It is usually drawn as a supply curve, with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal, for one seller or a whole market. Supply depends on the good's own price, the prices of related goods, production costs, technology and sellers' expectations. These work in two different ways. A change in the good's own price moves sellers along the curve. A change in anything else shifts the whole curve, as when a costlier ingredient shifts it left. Behind the curve sits cost. A firm's short-run supply curve traces its extra cost per unit ({{ref:nature-econ-347}}) above the point where it would shut down. The market supply curve adds up what all firms would supply at each price. Where there are no externalities, the curve shows the social cost of each extra unit. It has limits, too. A supply curve exists only under {{ref:nature-econ-353}}. A lone seller has none, because it picks price and quantity together.

nature-econ-360.title: Supply and demand: the model behind prices
nature-econ-360.text: In the fourteenth century the scholar Ibn Taymiyyah wrote that when desire for goods rises while availability falls, the price rises. Modern economics made that insight its theoretical foundation: the model of supply and demand. It explains how a market sets prices. The price moves until the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer, and the equilibrium is the price and quantity where the two curves cross. Each curve has a logic. Consumers buy another unit as long as its value to them is more than its price, so the buyers' curve slopes downward. When many small firms compete, supply follows the extra cost of each unit: firms produce more as long as that cost is below the market price. Augustin Cournot first drew the buyers' curve in 1838, Fleeming Jenkin added the sellers' curve in 1870, and Alfred Marshall popularized both in 1890. The model reaches beyond goods. Workers supply labor, businesses demand it, and the equilibrium price is the wage rate. Where a single seller or buyer can sway prices, other models fit better. Critics question the model itself. Sraffa doubted the consistency of supply curves drawn for a single market. Post-Keynesians argue it fails to explain prices that firms set by adding a mark-up to their costs.

nature-econ-335.title: Equilibrium: when the market stops moving
nature-econ-335.text: Economists borrowed equilibrium from the physical sciences, where balanced forces mean that nothing further changes. Economic equilibrium is a state in which the forces of supply and demand balance, so prices and quantities stop changing. In a market equilibrium, competition sets a price at which the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers produce. That price is called the competitive or market-clearing price, and it tends to stay put unless demand or supply changes. Pull the price away and forces push it back. A price above equilibrium creates a glut that pushes prices down. A price below it creates a shortage that pushes prices up. When the conditions of demand or supply change, the curves shift and the equilibrium moves. Huw Dixon proposed three properties: agents' behavior is consistent, no agent wants to change its behavior, and the outcome comes from a stable dynamic process. Balance is not the same as good. Paul Samuelson and others warn that a food market can be in equilibrium while people starve. During Ireland's Great Famine of 1845–52, food was exported while people starved, because the market price was above what Irish farmers could afford. Some economists also challenge the classical view that markets left alone always clear, pointing to lasting unemployment and credit rationing.

nature-econ-388.title: The law of demand: higher price, fewer buyers
nature-econ-388.text: Charles Davenant stated it in 1699: all else being equal, people buy less of a good when its price rises and more when it falls. This is the law of demand. It says only which way quantity moves when price changes, not by how much. Alfred Marshall drew it as a graph and joined it with supply in his Principles of Economics in 1890. The graph, covered in {{ref:nature-econ-371}}, puts quantity on the horizontal axis and price on the vertical, and it slopes downward. A price change moves buyers along that curve. Changes in the number of buyers, income, tastes, prices of related goods or expectations shift the whole curve. Together with its partner on the sellers' side ({{ref:nature-econ-391}}), the law fixes the equilibrium price and quantity. It has exceptions: Giffen goods, status goods ({{ref:nature-econ-390}}), necessities, and cases where buyers expect prices to keep changing.

nature-econ-378.title: Free markets: prices without government steering
nature-econ-378.text: To classical economists such as Adam Smith, a free market meant one free of privilege, exclusive selling rights and artificial scarcities. Today the term means an economic system without government steering. Prices of goods and services are set by the supply and demand of buyers and sellers. Its supporters contrast it with a regulated market, where government steps into supply and demand through taxes or rules. A free market does not demand competition as such, but it does demand that new sellers be free to enter. Free markets are usually linked with capitalism, but they have also featured in some forms of market socialism. In practice governments usually step in to cut harms such as planet-warming emissions, sometimes by using markets, as in carbon trading. The arguments run both ways. Critics say real free markets drift toward price-fixing and dominant single sellers, and unequal bargaining power, which led to measures such as US antitrust law. Coase, Friedman, von Mises and Hayek replied that markets can absorb or adjust to supposed market failures.

nature-econ-374.title: Elasticity: how strongly one thing responds to another
nature-econ-374.text: If buyers' elasticity for a good is −2, a 10% price rise cuts the quantity they buy by 20%. Elasticity measures how much one economic variable responds to a change in another: the percentage change in one divided by the percentage change in the other. The main kinds track how buying responds to price and to income, how selling responds to price, and how buying one good responds to another good's price. Elasticity helps explain who bears indirect taxes and how welfare is split among consumers, producers and government. It also guides pricing. Seller revenue is highest at unit elasticity, so a firm should raise its price when demand is inelastic and cut it when demand is elastic. Time is arguably the biggest influence on supply: the longer suppliers have to respond, the more supply changes. Goods made from scarce resources from nature, such as gasoline, respond poorly, so rising demand drives their prices up. Alfred Marshall first described price elasticity informally in his Principles of Economics of 1890.

nature-econ-371.title: The demand curve: buying at every price
nature-econ-371.text: A demand curve is a graph showing how much of a good people will buy at each price. Price goes on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal. It can show one consumer's demand or, added up across everyone, a whole market's. It normally slopes down because of the law of demand. Exceptions include status goods ({{ref:nature-econ-390}}), Giffen goods and speculative bubbles. The curve moves in two ways. A price change moves buyers along it, while a change in anything else, such as income, related goods' prices, population or expectations, shifts the whole curve. When incomes rise, demand for normal goods shifts out and demand for inferior goods shifts in. If hamburgers get dearer, demand for chicken, a substitute, shifts out, while demand for ketchup, a complement, shifts in. One practical snag remains. Demand curves are estimated statistically from past data, yet only one point on the curve can be observed at any one time.

nature-econ-363.title: Competition: the contest for customers
nature-econ-363.text: In 1776 Adam Smith described competition as steering productive resources to their most valued uses and encouraging efficiency. Competition is the contest among firms for customers and limited resources, fought with price, product, promotion and place. It arises from scarcity: there is never enough to satisfy every human want. Classical economists held that it pushes firms to develop new products and technologies, giving consumers more choice and better goods. More choice usually means lower prices than when one or a few firms dominate. How much competition a market has depends on the number of firms, barriers to entry, information and access to resources. Share and foreign-exchange markets are usually seen as close to perfect, while real estate is a very imperfect market. For a few goods, having many firms is itself inefficient, because competition duplicates costs that do not vary with output; {{ref:nature-econ-350}} covers these cases. Economists still debate how relevant the textbook ideal of {{ref:nature-econ-353}} is to real markets, and whether it should serve as the benchmark.

nature-econ-358.title: Price elasticity of demand: how buyers react to price
nature-econ-358.text: Suppose a price rises $5 from $100 and sales fall 20 tons from 200 tons. Quantity drops 10% while price rises 5%, so the price elasticity of demand is −2. That number measures how strongly the quantity people buy responds to a change in price: the percentage change in quantity for a one percent change in price. Demand is inelastic when the elasticity is below one in absolute value and elastic when it is above one. Close substitutes make demand more elastic. Necessities such as insulin, and broad categories such as food in general, are less elastic. Elasticity also grows with time: after a lasting fuel price rise, more people switch to carpooling or public transport. For inelastic goods a price rise increases revenue, while for elastic goods it lowers revenue. Revenue peaks where elasticity is exactly one. The measure also predicts who bears a tax. With perfectly inelastic demand consumers pay all of it; with perfectly elastic demand firms pay all of it. Alfred Marshall is credited with defining it in his Principles of Economics of 1890.

nature-econ-387.title: The invisible hand: self-interest serving the public
nature-econ-387.text: Adam Smith used the phrase just once in The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759) and once in The Wealth of Nations. He wrote of "an" invisible hand, never "the." It became his most famous metaphor: the way free markets can lead self-interested people to benefit the public without meaning to. In The Wealth of Nations it appears in a chapter about where merchants invest their capital, not about free trade. Paul Samuelson's 1948 textbook popularized the phrase and gave it a new meaning: that free markets regulate themselves and reach outcomes government cannot improve. The idea is a central justification for the hands-off thinking behind neoclassical economics. Joseph Stiglitz argues the hand often seems invisible because it is not there. With externalities, markets on their own produce too much pollution, which is why environmental economics deals largely with market failures. Stiglitz, Piketty and others argue that markets often fail to turn self-interest into social good. Scholars also disagree about what Smith himself meant.

nature-econ-385.title: Income elasticity of demand: what richer people buy
nature-econ-385.text: As people grow richer, their spending on food grows more slowly than their income, an observation called Engel's law. Income elasticity of demand measures this kind of response: how strongly the quantity of a good people buy responds to a change in their income. It is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in income. If a 10% rise in income lifts demand by 20%, it is 2.0. Normal goods score positive and inferior goods negative; below 1 marks a necessity and above 1 a luxury. Food as a whole lies between zero and one. Estimates for gasoline in developed economies range from 0.66 to 1.26. Elasticities for food and energy tend to fall as incomes rise: for cereals, from 0.62 in Tanzania to 0.05 in the United States. As economies get richer, spending shifts toward services, which need fewer commodities to produce. The pattern matters for nature. Most measures of environmental damage rise with income, though with an income elasticity below one.

nature-econ-463.title: Comparative statics: before-and-after snapshots
nature-econ-463.text: Comparative statics compares two economic outcomes, one before and one after a change in some outside factor, once the economy has settled into its new equilibrium. It compares the two snapshots but does not study the path between them. Economists use it to study changes in supply and demand in one market, and changes in government taxing, spending or money policy for a whole economy. The method had been drawn in graphs since at least the 1870s; John R. Hicks (1939) and Paul A. Samuelson (1947) formalized it. Results usually come from a linear approximation of the equilibrium equations, which assumes the equilibrium is stable. Because of that approximation, they hold only for very small changes. For models of steady growth, the counterpart is comparative dynamics. Two mathematical results support the method. The envelope theorem describes how the value of an optimal solution changes with a parameter. Claude Berge's 1963 maximum theorem describes when the optimal solution varies continuously with the parameters.

nature-econ-408.title: Price signals: what a price tells people
nature-econ-408.text: When a product runs short and its price rises, people pay more attention to it and produce more of it. That is a price signal at work: the information a price carries to buyers and sellers, telling them to supply or demand more or less of something. Prices coordinate what is produced, how it is produced and what resources are used. Friedrich Hayek argued that prices let people share knowledge spread among many others and coordinate their separate actions. Signals can be weakened. Dominant single sellers, price-fixing groups and dominant single buyers can set prices that do not reflect production costs. Credit bubbles and speculation can distort signals, leading to waste and financial crises. Signals can also be added. Taxes on fuel make consumers aware of hidden costs such as planet-warming gases and other pollution. Where signals are missing, behavior barely responds. Electricity users react little to price in the short run because they do not face the actual cost of production at each moment.

nature-econ-395.title: Market economies: letting prices guide production
nature-econ-395.text: In a market economy, strong demand with limited supply pushes prices up and invites more production. That price system is the heart of the definition. A market economy is one in which decisions about investment, production and distribution are guided by prices set through supply and demand. Prices signal people to adjust what they produce and invest. Market economies range from barely regulated free-market systems to interventionist ones, where governments correct market failures and promote welfare. All of them need clearly defined, enforceable rules of ownership ({{ref:nature-econ-621}}), though these need not be private: co-operatives and state firms can also trade in markets. Governments have several tools. They can set maximum or minimum prices, such as a lowest legal wage, or use taxes on harmful side effects ({{ref:nature-pol-088}}) to deal with externalities. Joseph Stiglitz argues that markets suffer from imperfect information and need government action to fix widespread market failures. A sustainable market economy tries to balance growth with environmental protection, using tax breaks, carbon trading and environmental rules.

nature-econ-402.title: Price controls: when governments set prices
nature-econ-402.text: Diocletian tried to cap the price of every commodity in the late 3rd century AD, with little success. Price controls are government-enforced limits on the prices that may be charged for goods and services, and they are ancient: the Code of Hammurabi set wages for shipbuilders. There are two main kinds. A ceiling ({{ref:nature-econ-400}}) sets the most that may be charged. A floor ({{ref:nature-econ-405}}) sets the least. Controls on rents and wages are well-known examples. Governments use them to keep goods affordable during shortages, to slow inflation, or to guarantee a minimum income to some providers. Controls are also one of the indirect ways governments subsidize energy. A cap set low tends to backfire. Keeping prices artificially low raises demand beyond what supply can meet, and shortages feed black markets with higher prices. During the 1973–74 Arab oil embargo, a US price cap below the market level led to long queues and gas stations running dry. Most Western economists say consumer price controls do not work, though since the 1990s wage floors have won strong support among some economists.

nature-econ-361.title: Shifts in supply and demand: when the whole curve moves
nature-econ-361.text: A cheaper way of growing wheat does something a change in the price of wheat cannot: it moves the entire supply curve. Shifts in supply and demand are changes in conditions other than a good's own price that move a whole curve, and so change the equilibrium price and quantity. Economists guard the language carefully. A movement along a curve is a "change in quantity demanded," while a shift of the whole curve is a "change in demand." Demand can rise because of changing tastes, higher incomes, price changes in substitutes and complements, expectations or more buyers. A rise in demand lifts both the equilibrium price and the quantity. Supply shifts work in either direction. The cheaper wheat-growing method shifts supply outward, lowering the price and raising the quantity sold. A rise in raw-material costs shifts supply to the left, so less is offered at every price.

nature-econ-407.title: The price mechanism: how prices share out resources
nature-econ-407.text: When the 1970s oil crisis drove oil prices up, several countries started producing their own oil. That response is the price mechanism at work: the way prices decide how resources are shared out and steer how much of each good is supplied and demanded. Prices match buyers and sellers in three ways: as an incentive, as a signal and as a way of rationing resources. The mechanism can be slow. Dearer fuel does not quickly cut demand, but over time it pushes firms to offer alternatives such as biodiesel and electric cars. Once competition settles into balance, the value society puts on a good equals the value of the resources used to make it, an ideal explored in {{ref:nature-econ-178}}. The mechanism takes many forms. In the form covered in {{ref:nature-econ-671}}, bidders compete and the highest bid wins. Cap-and-trade for planet-warming gases applies the idea to emissions, as the US did earlier with sulfur dioxide, cutting overall smog. Ludwig von Mises argued that planned economies reject the price mechanism and so cannot allocate resources rationally.

nature-econ-413.title: Total cost: the full bill for making output
nature-econ-413.text: Total cost is the lowest cost of producing a given amount of output. It is made up of costs that vary with output plus costs that do not. Labor and raw materials change with output; buildings and machinery do not, in the short term. In economics, total cost includes the opportunity cost of every input, the benefit of its next-best use. The extra total cost of one more unit gets its own entry, {{ref:nature-econ-347}}. Given time, the bill can shrink. Long-run total cost is generally lower than short-run, because the amount of capital can be chosen to suit the output.

nature-econ-347.title: Marginal cost: the price of one more unit
nature-econ-347.text: To make one more car, a carmaker needs more labor and parts, but not a new factory building. Marginal cost is that extra total cost of producing one more unit of output. It counts only costs that change with output. It differs from the cost per unit on average, which is total cost divided by the number of units made. Because costs that do not vary with output stay put, doubling them leaves marginal cost, and the profit-maximizing price and quantity, unchanged. Textbooks expect marginal cost to rise in the short run, as more labor and materials press against a fixed building and machinery. A competitive firm keeps producing as long as the sale price exceeds marginal cost, stopping where the two are equal. On a graph, the marginal cost curve crosses the average-cost curves at their lowest points. Where growing bigger cuts unit costs ({{ref:nature-econ-303}}), pricing at marginal cost fails to cover total costs and so needs a subsidy. The textbook picture is disputed. In a survey of 200 executives, 11% said their marginal costs rose with output, 48% said they were constant and 41% said they fell. Many empirical studies likewise find marginal cost constant or falling for most firms.

nature-econ-409.title: Profit: what is left after every cost
nature-econ-409.text: Economists usually assume firms try to maximize profit, so they define it carefully. Profit is what a business has left from its revenue after paying the total costs of its inputs, counting both explicit and implicit costs. Accounting profit subtracts only the explicit costs on a firm's books. Economic profit also subtracts implicit costs, so it is smaller. The break-even case ({{ref:nature-econ-354}}) is when revenue just equals total costs, so economic profit is zero: the least a firm needs to stay in a competitive industry. Competition erodes anything more. In a perfectly competitive market, economic profit draws in new firms until prices fall and the profit disappears in the long run. Profit lasts only in markets with one or a few dominant sellers. Barriers to entry protect it: patents, rights to land and rules on how land is used. Competition laws aim to stop powerful firms from building artificial barriers to protect their profits. Profit is greatest where the revenue from one more unit equals its marginal cost. A wider measure, social profit, adds or subtracts the externalities, such as pollution, and the gains to buyers that a firm's activity creates.

nature-econ-349.title: Monopoly: the market with one seller
nature-econ-349.text: The word first appears in Aristotle's Politics, describing Thales of Miletus cornering the market in olive presses. A monopoly is a market in which a single person or company is the only supplier of a particular good or service. With no competition and no close substitutes, it can charge a price well above its marginal cost and earn high profits. Size is not what defines it: a small business can still raise prices in a small market. Its power comes from barriers to entry, which may be economic, legal or deliberate. A monopolist does not simply charge the highest price. It picks the output where the revenue from one more sale equals the cost of making it, aiming at the largest total profit. Compared with a market of many small competitors it sells less at a higher price. The trades it forgoes are a pure loss to society ({{ref:nature-econ-345}}). Contestable-market theory adds that a monopoly may act as if it faced competition when entry barriers are low. Governments respond by taking monopoly profits, breaking up the firm or changing rules to curb anti-competitive behavior.

openers.markets-prices-and-surplus: A market is any arrangement that lets buyers and sellers exchange goods, services and information, and a price is the sum both sides will accept. On one side stands demand, the quantity people are willing and able to buy at various prices. On the other stands supply, the amount sellers are willing and able to offer. The basic model of supply and demand says the price moves until those two amounts match, a balance economists call equilibrium. This chapter follows that model from the law of demand to elasticity, competition and the free market.
